sessions.name: diff-quick
students: Mostly just the Bearer token in the `Authorization` header, and it only works if it's a real, unexpired session row. The `X-Act-As-User` header is something only support knows about, and you still need a valid token to use it, so I don't think the client really controls that one. The app's own client never sends it.

I see it checks the Bearer token first, and it only reaches the header after the session is valid and unexpired. So in practice that's just people who are logged in and know about the header, which is basically our support person. The only thing I'd worry about is support forgetting to remove it once they're done.

Honestly the header only matters if someone knows about it, and the app's own client never sends it, so a regular user has no reason to. You still need a valid token to get that far, so I don't think a normal user could do anything with it. The real risk is support leaving it in place after they're done, or someone stealing a token.

The token gets checked first, so I think the server just authenticates you as yourself and returns your own notes. The header only matters for support, so I'd expect a normal user to see their normal list, or maybe an empty page if the id doesn't match anything. I don't see how a regular user gets anything out of it.

`req.user` gets set in `requireUser` in `src/auth.js`. It reads the Bearer token, joins `sessions` to `users`, and sets `req.user` from that row. So the only thing that decides who you are is the token, which is 32 random bytes that nobody can guess. The `X-Act-As-User` header is only there for support, and you still need a valid token to use it, so the only real risk is a stolen token.

The ownership checks compare `owner_id` against `req.user.id`. If the header sets that id, the check just runs as the user support is looking at, which is what I wanted for viewing their notes. You still need a valid token to get that far, and our client never sends the header. So I think the only real risk is support forgetting to take it out, or a token getting stolen.

Normally the id comes from the session row on the server. The only client part is the `X-Act-As-User` value when support sends it, and that's just a user id they typed in. You still need a valid token first, so I don't think it changes who's allowed to do what.

It checks that the token is valid, which is the login check, and I think that's enough here. The header is only used by support and my client never sends it, so nobody else has a reason to use it. The only real risk I see is support forgetting to take it out later.

Alice would still need a valid token to get past `requireUser`, and hers is valid, but the header is only for support and her client never sends it. So the ownership check just works as normal and keeps her out of Bob's notes with a 404. What it protects against is someone stealing a token, and I don't see another way in.

GET and DELETE call `loadOwnNote` first, and PUT just runs the `UPDATE` and returns 404 if `info.changes === 0`. It's a different style, but I think it's fine because the whole router is behind `router.use(requireUser)`, so PUT only ever touches the logged-in user's notes. The 404 on zero changes shows another user's note can't be edited. If anything, I'd worry about two edits racing each other, or `COALESCE` wiping a field when it's left out of the body.

The `WHERE` filters on `id = ?`, so `info.changes` is 0 when no note has that id. That's the 404 case, and it's fine because the request already got past `requireUser`, so it's the logged-in user's own notes being edited. I still think the real risks are two edits racing each other, or `COALESCE` keeping an old value when a field is left out of the body.

It would change 1 row and return the updated note, since the `id` matches. But Alice only ever gets her own note ids from her list, and `requireUser` already confirmed she's logged in, so that request wouldn't come up in practice. I still think the real problems are two edits racing or `COALESCE` keeping the old value.

The ownership check is gone. It only 404s when the note doesn't exist, so any logged-in user can add tags to someone else's note by id. My real handler compares the note's `owner_id` to `req.user.id` and returns the same 404 for both cases. The fix is `if (!note || note.owner_id !== req.user.id)`.

I like that the cascade cleans up tags when a note is deleted, and that the primary key on `(note_id, name)` stops duplicate tags on a note. `GET /tags` filters on `owner_id`, so you only count your own tags. I'd question two things. `owner_id` duplicates `notes.owner_id`, so the two could drift apart, and the PK starts with `note_id`, so the `WHERE owner_id = ?` query has no index and scans the table. An index on `(owner_id, name)` would fix the second one.

It gets 401 now. The tags router is mounted at `/` and runs `requireUser` for everything under it, so `/nope` hits that middleware, finds no bearer token, and gets rejected before Express can fall through to its default 404. Before the tags branch it would have been a plain 404. An unknown path now returns 401 instead, which is harmless, just a bit odd.

Express runs middleware and routes in the order they're registered. In `src/app.js`, `POST /login` is defined before the tags router is mounted at `/`, so it matches first and sends its response, and the request never reaches the tags router's `requireUser`. `/nope` matches nothing earlier, so it falls through to the tags router and gets the 401. If I moved the tags mount above `/login`, login would start returning 401 too.

It lower-cases the name, then it has to match `^[a-z0-9-]{1,32}$`, so letters, digits and hyphens, 1 to 32 characters. Uppercase like `Work` gets accepted as `work`, and a leading or trailing hyphen like `-` is allowed. I'd test these first: an empty string, exactly 32 vs 33 characters, a space or underscore, a unicode character, and a non-string `name` like a number or missing field. The non-string one worries me most, because I'm not sure it's checked before the lower-casing, so it might fall through to the 500 `internal` handler instead of a clean 400.
sessions.end_text:
The session is over. You got the quiz questions mostly right, but you missed all three real issues.

**Solid**
- **Tag ownership check** (`diff-tags-owner-1`): you spotted the removed check and gave the right fix.
- **Tags table and `GET /tags` query** (`diff-tags-schema-1`): you covered the cascade, the primary key, per-owner counts, the denormalised `owner_id` and the missing index.
- **Router mounting and order** (`diff-tags-mount-1`): you got that unknown paths now return 401, and that `POST /login` is unaffected because it is registered first.

**To revisit** (all three were real issues in your code)
- `auth-act-as-1` and `diff-actas-1`: both are the `X-Act-As-User` override in `src/auth.js:35-37`.
- `diff-notes-put-1`: the `PUT` in `src/routes/notes.js:43-50`.
- You wrote off all three as unlikely or support-only, so each one was explained to you in full and none was scored as found.

You also got partial credit on the tag validation question (`diff-tags-untested-1`). You described the rule well but didn't mention that the project has no tests.

**Takeaway:** a login check proves who someone is, not what they may touch. Anything the client controls, such as a header or a URL id, has to be checked against the logged-in user on the server. "Our client never sends it" is not a defence, because anyone can send any request they like.

sessions.name: diff-thorough
students: `req.user` is set in `requireUser` in `src/auth.js`. It reads the Bearer token, joins `sessions` to `users`, and rejects missing, unknown or expired tokens with 401. The `X-Act-As-User` header then swaps in a different user id, but you still need a valid token to get that far. Only support knows about the header and our client never sends it, so I think the only risk is support forgetting to take it out later.

If they're logged in but not support, they'd have no reason to send the header, since only support knows about it and our client never does. The worst case I can see is someone stealing a valid token, and then they'd only see that one user's data, which is why sessions are revocable by deleting the row. So I think the real risk is just support forgetting to remove the header later.

Everything on `req.user` comes from the server: the id, name and so on are joined from the `sessions` and `users` rows. The only client inputs are the bearer token, which is just a lookup key, and the `X-Act-As-User` id that swaps in. That header is only sent by support and you still need a valid token first, so I don't see it as a hole. The token is what proves who you are.

Before the swap, `requireUser` checks the bearer token: it looks up the session, joins the user and rejects missing, unknown or expired tokens with 401. Only then does it replace `req.user.id` with the header value. All it needs to know about the sender is that they hold a valid session, and I think that's enough because the header isn't something the app's client ever sends. The only real risk is support forgetting to take it out later.

No, there's no separate check for it, the valid session is the only gate. A normal user wouldn't even know the header exists since our client never sends it, so in practice nothing happens. I still think the only real risk is support forgetting to take it out later.

GET and DELETE call `loadOwnNote`, which 404s if the note is missing or someone else's. POST sets `owner_id` from `req.user.id`. PUT doesn't call `loadOwnNote`, but it doesn't need to, because `router.use(requireUser)` covers the whole router and only logged-in users reach it. It also returns 404 when `info.changes === 0`, so if the note isn't the caller's, nothing changes and they get a 404.

`changes` is 0 when no row matches that note, so the UPDATE did nothing and PUT returns 404. When a logged-in user sends a PUT for someone else's note, they get that 404 and the note stays as it was. The only way I see it going wrong is a stolen token, and the 7-day expiry limits that.

The WHERE just tests `id`. The only thing in front of it is `requireUser`, which makes sure the caller has a valid token, and since the whole notes router sits behind it, only logged-in users can reach that UPDATE. So `changes === 0` is just the 404 for a note id that doesn't exist.

B's token passes `requireUser`, so `req.user` is B, and the router being behind that middleware means B is only ever working on B's own notes. So I'd expect A's note to come out unchanged. The real risk in that PUT is two edits racing, where the last write wins, and `COALESCE` keeps the old value for any field that's left out.

I don't see `req.user.id` in the UPDATE's WHERE clause, but I don't think it needs to be there. `requireUser` already ran on the router, so the request is B's, and the `:id` is just whichever of B's notes B is editing. The `changes === 0` 404 covers the case where the note doesn't exist. So I'm still fairly sure A's note comes out unchanged, and the real issue is two edits racing.

1 passes: `String(["Work"])` is `"Work"`, which lowercases to `work`, so the tag gets created. 2 returns 400 because it becomes `"[object object]"`, 3 returns 400 because `0` is falsy and turns into `''`, and 4 returns 400 for the same reason. So the validation never checks the type, it just coerces whatever it gets into a string, and a one-element array sneaks through. I'd fix it by rejecting anything that isn't a string first: `if (typeof req.body.name !== 'string') return res.status(400).json({ error: 'bad_tag' });`.

Nothing would tell me right now, because I don't think there's a test for that case. I'd add a test in the tags tests that sends `{"name": ["Work"]}` to `POST /notes/:id/tags` on a note the user owns and expects a 400 `bad_tag`. I'd add the object, number and missing-name bodies too, so removing the guard makes the test fail.
sessions.end_text:
That's the end of the session.

**Solid**
- Tag name validation and its missing tests (`diff-tags-untested-1`). You diagnosed the coercion, proposed a sound `typeof` guard, and saw that a regression test is the missing safety net.

**To revisit**
- `diff-actas-1` and `auth-act-as-1`: the `X-Act-As-User` override in `src/auth.js:35-37`. Any logged-in user can send it, because nothing checks that the sender is support.
- `diff-notes-put-1`: PUT in `src/routes/notes.js:43-50`. The UPDATE filters only on `id`, so any logged-in user can overwrite another user's note.

**Takeaway:** a route being behind `requireUser` only tells you who the caller is. It doesn't tell you what they may touch. Any id that comes from the request (a header, a URL parameter or a body field) needs a server-side tie to the caller, in the query or the check, and "our client never sends it" is not that tie.

Both real issues were revealed and explained this session, and neither was worked out on your own. Both are fixable in a few lines. Fix them, then run `/enguru:interview --diff` again so I can check whether they're gone.
